segments.chapter: Harlem youth, Monk and Bird, and Greensboro
segments.title: Freddie Webster's sound and Miles's debt to him
segments.summary: McLean describes Freddie Webster's sound as a big red ball and hears Miles absorbing it.

segments.chapter: Harlem youth, Monk and Bird, and Greensboro
segments.title: Following Bird to the Three Deuces on 52nd Street
segments.summary: With his mother's curfew in force, McLean and friends trail Bird into 52nd Street, and Bird gets them let in to stand by the door and hear Salt Peanuts; his mother's name was Alpha Omega.

segments.chapter: Harlem youth, Monk and Bird, and Greensboro
segments.title: Break in the recording
segments.summary: Brower suggests stopping and the recording is interrupted.

segments.chapter: Harlem youth, Monk and Bird, and Greensboro
segments.title: Maxton and Greensboro: North Carolina family and summers
segments.summary: Prompted by a question about the North Carolina migration stream, McLean recalls Maxton, his grandmother's house in Greensboro, cousins, his name Lenwood, the news of John McLean's death in 1939.

segments.chapter: Harlem youth, Monk and Bird, and Greensboro
segments.title: The grandmother's Pentecostal church versus Abyssinian
segments.summary: McLean describes the Pentecostal service with tambourines and a preacher building like a saxophone solo.

segments.chapter: Harlem youth, Monk and Bird, and Greensboro
segments.title: Summers in Greensboro: cowboy movies and games with cousins
segments.summary: Saturday cowboy films in the black theater, rolling tires, slingshots and errands on his bike.

segments.chapter: Harlem youth, Monk and Bird, and Greensboro
segments.title: How church music shaped his sense of rhythm, and Mingus
segments.summary: Church rhythm and spirituals lie at the root of his musical understanding, along with movie music, and he heard that gospel feeling in Mingus's pieces.

segments.chapter: Harlem youth, Monk and Bird, and Greensboro
segments.title: Going back to Greensboro for college in 1954
segments.summary: To please his mother he went to North Carolina A&T though he had already recorded with Miles; he met Dannie Richmond's circle and T. J. Anderson.

segments.chapter: Harlem youth, Monk and Bird, and Greensboro
segments.title: His first record, with Charlie Singleton's rhythm-and-blues band
segments.summary: McLean played baritone on Camel Walkin' for Singleton in New York around 1947-48, before Dig.

segments.chapter: Harlem youth, Monk and Bird, and Greensboro
segments.title: North Carolina musicians and the migrant stream
segments.summary: Brower proposes a pattern of North Carolina origins among jazz players; McLean sees a vortex drawing musicians to the same place.

segments.chapter: Harlem youth, Monk and Bird, and Greensboro
segments.title: A&T's lack of interest in jazz and playing r&b locally
segments.summary: A&T did not want jazz; he gave up music, studied history and dropped out, playing weekend r&b bands where B. B. King passed through.

segments.chapter: Alto sound, teachers and fellow altoists
segments.title: Making the alto sound like a tenor, and falling for Bird and Stitt
segments.summary: McLean disliked sweet alto players, modelled himself on Lester Young and Dexter, then found Parker, Sonny Stitt and Rudy Williams.

segments.chapter: Alto sound, teachers and fellow altoists
segments.title: Saxophone teachers: Foots Thomas, Cecil Scott, Andy Brown, Joe Napoleon
segments.summary: He studied briefly with several teachers but quit when they pushed a stiff classical embouchure.

segments.chapter: Alto sound, teachers and fellow altoists
segments.title: Sound, mouthpieces and his Selmer
segments.summary: McLean says his tone is a mystery that stays the same whatever the reed, mouthpiece or horn; he has used a Selmer since 1965.

segments.chapter: Alto sound, teachers and fellow altoists
segments.title: Discovering Sonny Stitt and meeting him in the neighborhood
segments.summary: He preferred Stitt to Bird for a year, then met Stitt on his block and let him change clothes at his mother's house.

segments.chapter: Alto sound, teachers and fellow altoists
segments.title: Sonny Stitt the gunslinger
segments.summary: Stitt cut McLean in jam sessions, battled him at Wolf Trap, kept calling for other keys and asking how many keys a saxophone has.

segments.chapter: Alto sound, teachers and fellow altoists
segments.title: Rudy Williams and the failed Oscar Pettiford audition
segments.summary: McLean met Rudy Williams at Bud's house, then flubbed charts at an Oscar Pettiford tryout and Pettiford replaced him with Williams.

segments.chapter: Alto sound, teachers and fellow altoists
segments.title: Phil Woods and meeting Cannonball Adderley at the Cafe Bohemia
segments.summary: Brower's list of altoists: McLean meets Cannonball when Oscar Pettiford puts them on stage together on Cannonball's first night in New York.

segments.chapter: Alto sound, teachers and fellow altoists
segments.title: Herbie Nichols
segments.summary: McLean sat in with Nichols and regards him as related to Monk, Bud and Ellington.

segments.chapter: Alto sound, teachers and fellow altoists
segments.title: Other altoists: Ornette, Bartz, Desmond, Coleman, Lake, Jenkins, Sharpe
segments.summary: McLean gives quick opinions on Ornette Coleman, Gary Bartz, Desmond, Kenny Garrett, Steve Coleman, Oliver Lake, John Jenkins and Cee Sharpe.

segments.chapter: Heroin and the Miles Davis years
segments.title: How he started using heroin
segments.summary: In 1946-47 drugs arrived in Harlem and his idols used them; left alone, he tried heroin at a dance and gradually increased use.

segments.chapter: Heroin and the Miles Davis years
segments.title: What a dollar bought
segments.summary: A capsule cost a dollar, and McLean explains the buying power of a dollar then.

segments.chapter: Heroin and the Miles Davis years
segments.title: Cocktail-sip dances inherited from Sonny Rollins
segments.summary: Rollins controlled the fraternity-dance jobs paying eight to twelve dollars; when he went away he passed them to McLean; Rollins returned transformed and joined Miles first.

segments.chapter: Heroin and the Miles Davis years
segments.title: Opening of the second day of interview
segments.summary: Brower opens Saturday July 21, 2001, saying the previous day's drug topic will be raised as the history unfolds, and asks what McLean got from Miles.

segments.chapter: Heroin and the Miles Davis years
segments.title: What he learned from Miles Davis
segments.summary: Miles taught him to study harmony and piano, economy and note choice, and the influence of Lester Young on Miles.

segments.chapter: Heroin and the Miles Davis years
segments.title: Miles on Sugar Hill and the square at 150th Street
segments.summary: Miles hung out with Sugar Hill peers like Roy Haynes, Sonny Rollins and Gil Coggins in a little park.

segments.chapter: Heroin and the Miles Davis years
segments.title: Miles strung out at the Downbeat, his father, and the Gil Coggins band
segments.summary: McLean recounts Miles's addiction, his father collecting him from the Downbeat, and Miles reforming a band at Birdland with Gil Coggins, whose chordal accompaniment won Miles over.

segments.chapter: Heroin and the Miles Davis years
segments.title: Rehearsing Miles's band and recommending Frank Strozier
segments.summary: Miles paid McLean to rehearse his tunes for Trane, Cannonball and Garland, and McLean sent Strozier in his place for California.

segments.chapter: Heroin and the Miles Davis years
segments.title: Miles's autobiography and the Yesterdays humiliation
segments.summary: McLean judges Miles's portrayal of him accurate and recalls Miles shaming him on stage over a tune he hadn't learned, while Art Blakey told him to go learn it.

segments.chapter: Heroin and the Miles Davis years
segments.title: Hanging out with Miles and bringing him home
segments.summary: Miles visits McLean's family apartment and puts his feet on the couch; they go to movies on 42nd Street.

segments.chapter: Wallington, Mingus and Blakey
segments.title: George Wallington's Bohemia quartet and Paul Chambers
segments.summary: McLean, Paul Chambers and Arthur Taylor worked in Wallington's band, recorded Bohemia After Dark, until Miles took Chambers.

segments.chapter: Wallington, Mingus and Blakey
segments.title: Order of Wallington, Mingus and Blakey; friendship with Art
segments.summary: McLean sorts out the sequence of his jobs and says Art Blakey has advised him since he was seventeen.

segments.chapter: Wallington, Mingus and Blakey
segments.title: The fight with Mingus in Cleveland
segments.summary: After McLean gives notice, Mingus punches him and McLean knifes him through his clothes; Mingus fires him and J. R. Monterose.

segments.chapter: Wallington, Mingus and Blakey
segments.title: Sneaking out of the Cleveland hotel and pawning a horn
segments.summary: Broke and snowed in, McLean and J. R. plot an escape from the hotel past a talkative desk clerk, then pawn a horn to get back to New York.

segments.chapter: Wallington, Mingus and Blakey
segments.title: Mingus as a drill instructor
segments.summary: McLean says he loved Mingus, who pushed him to find his own sound and taught by ear from the piano.

segments.chapter: Wallington, Mingus and Blakey
segments.title: Pithecanthropus Erectus rehearsed in front of audiences
segments.summary: Mingus ran the piece repeatedly on the bandstand as a workshop, stretching and cutting chords, which opened McLean to new composition ideas.

segments.chapter: Wallington, Mingus and Blakey
segments.title: Mingus's politics and the night of Emmett Till
segments.summary: At the Bohemia Mingus dedicated tunes to Emmett Till all night.

segments.chapter: Wallington, Mingus and Blakey
segments.title: Blakey's anger, the union and Mingus's apology
segments.summary: Art is outraged when Mingus hits him, the union wants Mingus thrown out, McLean refuses to sign and Mingus later reconciles, writing Portrait of Jackie.

segments.chapter: Wallington, Mingus and Blakey
segments.title: Leaving Mingus for Art Blakey's Pittsburgh trip
segments.summary: Blakey, seeing the horn is not even McLean's, offers to buy him one and takes him to Pittsburgh in his Cadillac.

segments.chapter: Wallington, Mingus and Blakey
segments.title: Pushed-back teeth and the advice to keep playing
segments.summary: Mingus's blow set his teeth back; he pulled them forward daily and Coltrane and Rollins told him to keep practicing.

segments.chapter: Wallington, Mingus and Blakey
segments.title: Mingus hunts for Jackie and the threatening telegram
segments.summary: Mingus searches McLean's apartment with Mal Waldron, Dollie turns him away, and a telegram threatens the East River.

segments.chapter: Wallington, Mingus and Blakey
segments.title: Learning to lead from Art Blakey
segments.summary: Blakey trained him to speak into the mic and manage the bandstand, praised his tone, and was privately Muslim.

segments.chapter: Bird memories, cabaret card and Prestige years
segments.title: The cabaret card loss and the Jackie McLean Fan Club
segments.summary: McLean lost his New York cabaret card after a drug arrest around 1956 and worked mostly fan-club concerts until he regained it around 1965 after The Connection.

segments.chapter: Bird memories, cabaret card and Prestige years
segments.title: Subbing for Bird and Bird sitting in at Birdland
segments.summary: McLean subbed for Bird twice and Bird calmed him when he first sat in on his band.

segments.chapter: Bird memories, cabaret card and Prestige years
segments.title: Easing Eric McPherson's nerves opposite Tony Williams
segments.summary: McLean has McPherson open the set with the drum intro of Rhythm of the Earth to get him comfortable.

segments.chapter: Bird memories, cabaret card and Prestige years
segments.title: Bird walks on stage with Miles's quintet, and the pocket game
segments.summary: Bird sat in on Groovin' High and sometimes took or gave money in McLean's pocket.

segments.chapter: Bird memories, cabaret card and Prestige years
segments.title: A day with Bird: Hot Lips Page's wake and the fish store
segments.summary: McLean spends a day walking Harlem with Bird, who admires an airplane and fish colors but never talks music.

segments.chapter: Bird memories, cabaret card and Prestige years
segments.title: Bird's death and the pawned saxophone
segments.summary: McLean and Bird parted badly after Bird pawned the horn they shared, with McLean's mouthpiece inside.

segments.chapter: Bird memories, cabaret card and Prestige years
segments.title: Marriage and children's birth years
segments.summary: McLean will not date his marriage and gives René's birth as 1946, Vernon's as 1948 and Melonae's as 1955.

segments.chapter: Bird memories, cabaret card and Prestige years
segments.title: Working behind singers Arthur Prysock and Jimmy Scott
segments.summary: Prysock taught him accompaniment by sitting him in a chair; Jimmy Scott let him play behind freely.

segments.chapter: Bird memories, cabaret card and Prestige years
segments.title: Pitch, bending notes and Lester Young
segments.summary: McLean says Scott and Billie Holiday taught him to shade pitch, and compares Hawkins's on-pitch approach with Pres's hanging notes.

segments.chapter: Bird memories, cabaret card and Prestige years
segments.title: Drums and piano as his other instruments
segments.summary: His first interest was drums after Gene Krupa, and he played drums when Billy Higgins was late; he plays piano for composing.

segments.chapter: Bird memories, cabaret card and Prestige years
segments.title: Sonny Stitt visits the Hartt School
segments.summary: Stitt insists McLean bring him to Hartt, where he talks to the class and plays piano and sings his songs.

segments.chapter: Bird memories, cabaret card and Prestige years
segments.title: President Clinton's visit to the Artists Collective
segments.summary: On November 4, 1999 the band played a Stitt tune for Clinton, who said he knew it from college.

segments.chapter: Bird memories, cabaret card and Prestige years
segments.title: Prestige as a music factory
segments.summary: Back to 1956, McLean recalls Bob Weinstock's no-rehearsal assembly-line sessions with two dates in a day versus Blue Note.

segments.chapter: Bird memories, cabaret card and Prestige years
segments.title: Money and an addict's daily routine
segments.summary: A leader got a $300 advance; McLean describes feeding the habit daily, hiding it from his family, and Dollie holding the family together.

segments.chapter: Bird memories, cabaret card and Prestige years
segments.title: Living on East Houston Street
segments.summary: In 1956-57 McLean lived on the Lower East Side where there was little music scene, and Bird visited.

segments.chapter: Bird memories, cabaret card and Prestige years
segments.title: Session length and twelve takes of Portrait of Jackie
segments.summary: A Prestige date ran about three hours; Mingus made McLean record Portrait of Jackie twelve times in a row and then used the first take.

segments.chapter: Bird memories, cabaret card and Prestige years
segments.title: The monster, Prestige versus Blue Note producers
segments.summary: Producers knew musicians needed money for their habits; Prestige lacked the love for music that Alfred Lion and Frank Wolff showed, who wired money when McLean was stranded in Lexington.

segments.chapter: Bird memories, cabaret card and Prestige years
segments.title: Prestige sidemen and the regional streams feeding New York
segments.summary: His habit left no musical circle beyond rehearsals; musicians from Detroit, Philadelphia, Chicago and New Jersey arrived as children of Bud and Bird.

segments.chapter: Blue Note, The Connection and Tony Williams
segments.title: Working in Philadelphia, Newark and Washington without a cabaret card
segments.summary: McLean played Philadelphia with Reggie Workman and young McCoy Tyner, a battle of the altos, and a Washington club the week of King's speech.

segments.chapter: Blue Note, The Connection and Tony Williams
segments.title: Joining The Connection at the Living Theater
segments.summary: In 1959 McLean signed with Blue Note and Freddie Redd brought him into the play The Connection, which ran several years and became Shirley Clarke's film.

segments.chapter: Blue Note, The Connection and Tony Williams
segments.title: Prestige dates remembered vaguely; Inding
segments.summary: McLean can barely recall Prestige sessions except experimental pieces like Inding with Elmo Hope.

segments.chapter: Blue Note, The Connection and Tony Williams
segments.title: John Jenkins and the Alto Madness date
segments.summary: Sonny Rollins warned him about Jenkins, who sat in with Mingus in Chicago; McLean got Weinstock to record the two-alto date; Arthur Phipps turned to photography.

segments.chapter: Blue Note, The Connection and Tony Williams
segments.title: Leaving Prestige for Blue Note
segments.summary: Alfred Lion and Frank Wolff found McLean at a club and signed him instead of extending his Prestige option.

segments.chapter: Blue Note, The Connection and Tony Williams
segments.title: Ray Draper and Webster Young
segments.summary: A teenaged Ray Draper introduced himself; McLean liked his writing, recorded him, and formed a band with Draper and trumpeter Webster Young.

segments.chapter: Blue Note, The Connection and Tony Williams
segments.title: Impressions of the Living Theater actors
segments.summary: McLean was at first dismissive of the actors' craft, then came to respect it, and says they travelled like gypsies across Europe.

segments.chapter: Blue Note, The Connection and Tony Williams
segments.title: Snowstorm departure and The Connection in London
segments.summary: An ambulance carries the cast to the ship; London's legal drug supply meant the play did not land.

segments.chapter: Blue Note, The Connection and Tony Williams
segments.title: Authenticity of the play and McLean's acting
segments.summary: He saw the play as about waiting for the connection, introducing him to theater, and he added lines.

segments.chapter: Blue Note, The Connection and Tony Williams
segments.title: Walter Davis high at The Connection
segments.summary: Walter Davis, subbing for Freddie Redd, was high and kept interrupting the play until they washed his face at intermission.

segments.chapter: Blue Note, The Connection and Tony Williams
segments.title: Tina Brooks as understudy
segments.summary: Freddie Redd approved Tina Brooks as McLean's understudy while he took other gigs.

segments.chapter: Blue Note, The Connection and Tony Williams
segments.title: Meeting teenage drummer Tony Williams in Boston
segments.summary: At Connolly's in Boston, a sixteen-year-old Tony Williams carries his bags and plays drums.

segments.chapter: Blue Note, The Connection and Tony Williams
segments.title: Bringing Tony to New York and escaping the hotel on Christmas Eve
segments.summary: McLean gets Tony into The Connection, has him buy gift boxes to smuggle luggage past the hotel desk, and flies home with him.

segments.chapter: Blue Note, The Connection and Tony Williams
segments.title: Tony living with the McLeans, his mother, and Miles taking him
segments.summary: Tony stayed a few weeks, moved to a loft, and Miles asked for him after hearing him.

segments.chapter: Blue Note, The Connection and Tony Williams
segments.title: Tony's concept of time and Jack DeJohnette
segments.summary: McLean admired Tony's open time, then replaced him with Jack DeJohnette.

segments.chapter: Blue Note, The Connection and Tony Williams
segments.title: The first Blue Note recording
segments.summary: McLean says New Soil, not Jackie's Bag, was his first Blue Note record.

segments.chapter: Blue Note, The Connection and Tony Williams
segments.title: Mr. Jones the Capuchin monkey
segments.summary: Taming the family monkey, who escaped and terrorised Dollie while McLean was on stage.

segments.chapter: Blue Note, The Connection and Tony Williams
segments.title: Control at Blue Note over music, titles and musicians
segments.summary: McLean cared only about choosing musicians and music; he named New Soil but hated Swing, Swing, Swing.

segments.chapter: Blue Note, The Connection and Tony Williams
segments.title: Pete LaRoca's open drumming
segments.summary: LaRoca played open-concept drums before Tony Williams.

segments.chapter: Blue Note, The Connection and Tony Williams
segments.title: No social circle around the Blue Note dates
segments.summary: The musicians were his choice but not friends; he and Walter Davis ran together while Donald Byrd and Paul Chambers were clean.

segments.chapter: Blue Note, The Connection and Tony Williams
segments.title: Stravinsky, Bartok and widening his writing
segments.summary: The day Bird died McLean bought Rite of Spring, which opened new directions, as it had for Tristano.

segments.chapter: Blue Note, The Connection and Tony Williams
segments.title: Writing Quadrangle, Inding and learning composition
segments.summary: McLean wrote by ear on the piano until about 1968, when he began to learn chord voicing.

segments.chapter: Lower East Side and Slug's
segments.title: How Slug's began on the Lower East Side
segments.summary: McLean persuaded the bar owners to try Sunday cocktail sips with flyers, which grew to six nights with his band.

segments.chapter: Lower East Side and Slug's
segments.title: Slug's phases and the Hampton Hawes trip
segments.summary: After the tape change Brower recalls Sun Ra Mondays; McLean left for San Francisco with Hampton Hawes and had Hank Mobley fill in.

segments.chapter: Lower East Side and Slug's
segments.title: The candy store on 3rd Street
segments.summary: McLean bought a candy store with his sons' savings and advertised it from the Slug's stage.

segments.chapter: Lower East Side and Slug's
segments.title: Musicians moving to the Lower East Side
segments.summary: As clubs like the Tin Palace and Five Spot appeared, musicians including Ed Blackwell moved downtown.

segments.chapter: Lower East Side and Slug's
segments.title: Painters and poets: Bob Thompson and Harvey Cropper
segments.summary: McLean's friendship with painter Bob Thompson shaped his view of the world, and he recalls Harvey Cropper in the Village around 1947.

segments.chapter: Lower East Side and Slug's
segments.title: Reading and time in jail
segments.summary: McLean became a reader in jail at The Tombs, Rikers Island and Hart Island.

segments.chapter: Lower East Side and Slug's
segments.title: Big George
segments.summary: Big George from Brooklyn rounded up audiences and helped on the road with Trane and McLean.

segments.chapter: Lower East Side and Slug's
segments.title: An all-night session before the Antioch festival
segments.summary: Brower recalls McLean keeping a room up all night before an early flight.

segments.chapter: Lower East Side and Slug's
segments.title: Drugs arriving on the Lower East Side and projects life
segments.summary: McLean once travelled uptown daily for drugs until supply came to the Lower East Side; he led local kids in a drum and bugle corps.

segments.chapter: Lower East Side and Slug's
segments.title: Mobilization for Youth drum and bugle corps and teaching René's friends
segments.summary: Under a Robert Kennedy-backed program McLean ran a drum and bugle corps and taught Bill Saxton, Fish and René.

segments.chapter: Lower East Side and Slug's
segments.title: Getting René onstage as a teenager
segments.summary: McLean left teenage René to close out nights with Billy Higgins's band.

segments.chapter: Lower East Side and Slug's
segments.title: Frank Mitchell
segments.summary: McLean recalls tenor player Frank Mitchell, René's age, who died strangely, from Lee Morgan's Sixth Sense.

segments.chapter: Lower East Side and Slug's
segments.title: Paid lessons while he stepped out to take care of business
segments.summary: Students paid for lessons in his house while he slipped out to get drugs.

segments.chapter: Later Blue Note years and ending the habit
segments.title: How his habit ended in 1965
segments.summary: After six months in jail, served four and a half, and help from a doctor who held him together with Dollie, he stopped; he was tired of jail.

segments.chapter: Later Blue Note years and ending the habit
segments.title: John Coltrane's death and overpracticing
segments.summary: Coltrane's death shocked McLean, who blames his marathon playing and practice rather than past addiction.

segments.chapter: Later Blue Note years and ending the habit
segments.title: Butch Warren
segments.summary: McLean hired Butch Warren after Webster Young recommended him; Warren later joined Monk and had problems.

segments.chapter: Later Blue Note years and ending the habit
segments.title: Let Freedom Ring and playing above the alto's range
segments.summary: Donald Byrd fell ill on the date so McLean cut it without trumpet, and used Illinois Jacquet's high register.

segments.chapter: Later Blue Note years and ending the habit
segments.title: The band with Grachan Moncur and Bobby Hutcherson
segments.summary: McLean's working quintet with Moncur, Hutcherson and Tony Williams replaced piano with vibes and played the East Coast including the Blue Coronet.

segments.chapter: Later Blue Note years and ending the habit
segments.title: Space and color from vibes and open accompanists
segments.summary: Hutcherson, LaMont Johnson and Herbie Nichols gave McLean space and color unlike straight-ahead Cedar Walton.

segments.chapter: Later Blue Note years and ending the habit
segments.title: Roy Haynes replaces Tony and favorite drummers
segments.summary: McLean praises Haynes as in Tony's roots and lists Carvin, Burrage, Eric McPherson, Nasheet Waits and Louis Nash.

segments.chapter: Later Blue Note years and ending the habit
segments.title: Titles and liner notes; a break
segments.summary: McLean says Let Freedom Ring, One Step Beyond and Destination Out titles were his; the recording is interrupted.

segments.chapter: Later Blue Note years and ending the habit
segments.title: Rudy Van Gelder's sound
segments.summary: Van Gelder's Blue Note recordings captured the music wonderfully, but later sessions disappointed.

segments.chapter: Later Blue Note years and ending the habit
segments.title: Larry Willis and Charles Tolliver
segments.summary: McLean met Tolliver when playing tenor with a hospital band; he likes pushing unfinished players off the high board as Miles did to him.

segments.chapter: Later Blue Note years and ending the habit
segments.title: The Ornette Coleman trumpet date
segments.summary: Ornette played trumpet on McLean's date, to the anger of Kenny Dorham and Lee Morgan.

segments.chapter: Later Blue Note years and ending the habit
segments.title: Conversion Point and going out
segments.summary: McLean says he cannot recall the piece and tries only to let the music evolve.

segments.chapter: Later Blue Note years and ending the habit
segments.title: Blue Note reissues and who owns his music
segments.summary: Blue Note issues unreleased sessions without asking him, and catalogs get sold on to firms like Coca Cola.

segments.chapter: Later Blue Note years and ending the habit
segments.title: Leaving Blue Note in 1968
segments.summary: When Lion and Wolff sold, McLean met George Butler and refused any relationship with the new company.

segments.chapter: Hartford, prison, theater and the Collective
segments.title: The penitentiary bandmaster job and the offer from Connecticut
segments.summary: Working as a bandmaster in a Manhattan penitentiary, McLean was approached by Connecticut to bring Afro-centric music to a university and consult for the arts commission.

segments.chapter: Hartford, prison, theater and the Collective
segments.title: Persuading Dollie to move to Hartford
segments.summary: Dollie, a staunch New Yorker, resisted until McLean found a house and an Atheneum job for her; he took a Hartford Dispensary counseling job.

segments.chapter: Hartford, prison, theater and the Collective
segments.title: Building the Hartt department and the Artists Collective
segments.summary: McLean founded the African-American Music department, now the Jackie McLean Institute, and helped start the Artists Collective.

segments.chapter: Hartford, prison, theater and the Collective
segments.title: Musicians on Rikers Island: Ike Quebec's band
segments.summary: McLean found Ike Quebec, Freddie Douglas and others locked up at Rikers, with a big band.

segments.chapter: Hartford, prison, theater and the Collective
segments.title: The Tombs and daily life on Rikers
segments.summary: The Tombs had no music and long lockup, while Rikers musicians rehearsed in the theater every day.

segments.chapter: Hartford, prison, theater and the Collective
segments.title: No writing in jail, and teaching novices
segments.summary: Jail did not inspire composing, and McLean taught beginners any instrument from a book.

segments.chapter: Hartford, prison, theater and the Collective
segments.title: Acting with the Living Theater and Julian Beck
segments.summary: McLean understudied for Living Theater parts, played a Chinese bartender in Paris, and remembers Julian Beck making him up.

segments.chapter: Hartford, prison, theater and the Collective
segments.title: Reading, ESP and Kahlil Gibran
segments.summary: McLean began reading in jail and heavily around 1970 for his classes, and wrote Khalil the Prophet.

segments.chapter: Hartford, prison, theater and the Collective
segments.title: Archie Shepp, teaching, and studying jazz history
segments.summary: Archie Shepp showed him that he could teach at a university; McLean then studied the music's history intensively from 1970 to 1972 without touching the saxophone.

segments.chapter: Hartford, prison, theater and the Collective
segments.title: Building the Artists Collective with integrity, and local resistance
segments.summary: The Collective repaid any stolen money itself and faced rivalry in Hartford's north end until people saw they would not give up.

segments.chapter: Hartford, prison, theater and the Collective
segments.title: Why the Collective teaches many arts: saving youth
segments.summary: McLean offered music, dance and visual arts to save youth and give direction; Eric LaSalle took his first drama lessons there.

segments.chapter: Hartford, prison, theater and the Collective
segments.title: Mentoring students: Steve Davis, Nat Reeves, the Rozies, Cindy Blackman
segments.summary: McLean mentors as Bud mentored him and lists graduates who now teach or play, including Cindy Blackman who took first drum lessons at the Collective.

segments.chapter: Hartford, prison, theater and the Collective
segments.title: His current role at the Jackie McLean Institute and being a stepchild at Hartt
segments.summary: McLean now teaches four weeks a semester, recalls being a stepchild in a European-music school, and the department becoming the school's pride.

segments.chapter: Hartford, prison, theater and the Collective
segments.title: How jazz education affects the music
segments.summary: Technology and universities give students far more than he had, producing many players and few spots, while Ken Burns brought attention.

segments.chapter: Hartford, prison, theater and the Collective
segments.title: The Ken Burns documentary
segments.summary: McLean refused to talk about Coltrane for Burns, disliked the choice of consultants like Wynton Marsalis, and noted missing voices like Benny Carter.

segments.chapter: Hartford, prison, theater and the Collective
segments.title: Lincoln Center concert of his compositions arranged for ten pieces
segments.summary: Slide Hampton and Walter Davis arranged his quintet pieces; Wynton Marsalis later asked for more but McLean hesitated.

segments.chapter: Hartford, prison, theater and the Collective
segments.title: Role of cultural institutions and funding
segments.summary: Brower and McLean discuss performance centers presenting artists of stature; McLean thinks enough wealth exists but is hard to raise.

segments.chapter: Hartford, prison, theater and the Collective
segments.title: The Artists Collective building
segments.summary: The building cost about eight million dollars, took Dollie fifteen years to raise, and opened in 1999 with parts unfinished.

segments.chapter: Copenhagen recordings, interests and views on the music
segments.title: Nils Winther secretly recording him in Copenhagen
segments.summary: McLean discovered Nils Winther recording him above the Montmartre and, urged by Kenny Drew, allowed him to start SteepleChase.

segments.chapter: Copenhagen recordings, interests and views on the music
segments.title: First SteepleChase albums and recording with Dexter Gordon
segments.summary: With Alex Riel on drums, McLean made live albums, and brought in Dexter, his giant, for The Meeting and The Source.

segments.chapter: Copenhagen recordings, interests and views on the music
segments.title: New York Calling, Antiquity with Michael Carvin and the Bartz date
segments.summary: SteepleChase recorded McLean's New York band; he describes Antiquity, a duo with Carvin with chants and found instruments, and recording with Gary Bartz in Copenhagen. McLean fell out with the label over unpaid royalties.

segments.chapter: Copenhagen recordings, interests and views on the music
segments.title: The Monuments record
segments.summary: He made Monuments to reach a bigger audience but disliked edited, patched solos and never did it again.

segments.chapter: Copenhagen recordings, interests and views on the music
segments.title: They All Seem to Disappear and Jelly Brown
segments.summary: McLean explains his childhood friend Walter Jelly Brown, who died strung out, and the kid material and pharaoh costume on the record.

segments.chapter: Copenhagen recordings, interests and views on the music
segments.title: Egyptology, jewelry and love of history
segments.summary: McLean's Egyptian and African jewelry reflects reading on pyramids, Napoleon and ancient African rulers.

segments.chapter: Copenhagen recordings, interests and views on the music
segments.title: Fascination with Hitler and the Second World War
segments.summary: McLean describes Hitler's charisma, the Nuremberg rallies, Skorzeny's rescue of Mussolini and German jet technology.

segments.chapter: Copenhagen recordings, interests and views on the music
segments.title: Brower and McLean discuss Hitler's regime and individual conscience
segments.summary: Brower cites Kershaw on Hitler dismantling the state, and wonders what he himself would have done.

segments.chapter: Copenhagen recordings, interests and views on the music
segments.title: African culture, the Dogon and Rhythm of the Earth
segments.summary: McLean is interested in Mali's cave drawings of the Dog Star, extraterrestrial life, and loves Julius Hemphill's Dogon A.D.

segments.chapter: Copenhagen recordings, interests and views on the music
segments.title: South Africa connection: René, Hotep Galeta and the 1993 tour
segments.summary: René went with Hugh Masekela and married in South Africa; McLean did a 1993 State Department tour of southern Africa and brought Hotep to Hartford.

segments.chapter: Copenhagen recordings, interests and views on the music
segments.title: How he has been treated in books
segments.summary: McLean comments on Four Lives in the Bebop Business, Hard Bop, Miles's autobiography and Sidran's Talking Jazz.

segments.chapter: Copenhagen recordings, interests and views on the music
segments.title: National Endowment for the Arts panels
segments.summary: McLean sat on NEA panels to keep Washington connections and bring funds to Hartt, the Collective and the Hartford Jazz Society.

segments.chapter: Copenhagen recordings, interests and views on the music
segments.title: Government subsidy for artists
segments.summary: McLean believes the government should fund musicians as Holland and France do, and that he creates best when comfortable.

segments.chapter: Copenhagen recordings, interests and views on the music
segments.title: Jazz survived hostility and racism
segments.summary: McLean says the music thrives despite attempts to exploit and kill it, and that racial separation among players is fading.

segments.chapter: Copenhagen recordings, interests and views on the music
segments.title: Stealing the music: Elvis, Whiteman and hip-hop's origin
segments.summary: Whites have come to dominate blues and jazz, but an idiom cannot be stolen; hip-hop arose when school music programs were cut.

segments.chapter: Copenhagen recordings, interests and views on the music
segments.title: Why the black community has drifted from jazz
segments.summary: McLean blames media promotion of other genres and says young people will always love Trane, Bird and Billie Holiday.

segments.chapter: Copenhagen recordings, interests and views on the music
segments.title: Relating to hip-hop
segments.summary: McLean likes hip-hop rhythms and designed Rhythm of the Earth to relate, and enjoys Roy Hargrove's genre mixing.

segments.chapter: Copenhagen recordings, interests and views on the music
segments.title: Younger generation and respect for elders
segments.summary: McLean is uncomfortable with young people dropping respect for elders and family, citing 'talk to the hand'.

segments.chapter: Copenhagen recordings, interests and views on the music
segments.title: The number 5 and close of the interview
segments.summary: McLean explains why he holds up his hand with five fingers; the interview closes with a transcriber note.
